newsitem.title: FRANCE: France allows pension fund capital payouts - Arthuis.
newsitem.headline: France allows pension fund capital payouts - Arthuis.

text.p: French Finance Minister Jean Arthuis confirmed on Thursday that pension funds being introduced in France would be allowed to make 20 percent of their payouts in a lump sum.
The finance ministry had originally proposed that payouts from pension funds be limited to annuities only.

Arthuis told parliament during a debate on a bill on pension funds that payouts could be made in a lump sum at retirement age, provided this represented no more than 20 percent of the money saved and no more than 100,000 francs.
Arthuis stressed however that the bulk of the payouts would be in annuities.
The announcement followed months of lobbying by banks, which favoured lump sum payouts, and insurance companies, which wanted money given out in the form of annuities.
Prime Minister Alain Juppe had suggested earlier this year that some payouts could be made in a lump sum, overturning the proposals made by his finance minister.
French government officials and members of parliament have held a series of talks over the last few weeks to iron out last minute amendments to the pension funds bill, drawn up in 1994.
Sources close to the talks had said beforehand that the bill was likely to allow up to 20 percent of payouts in a lump sum.
They also said funds were likely to see their investment in bonds capped at around 60 percent of their assets.
Arthuis made no mention of this latter requirement in a brief statement to parliament.
But he said employee contributions to pension funds would be exempt from income tax up to a limit of five percent of gross salary.
Employer contributions would be exempt from social security contributions up to a limit of 4,000 francs a year or two percent of annual salary, he said.
The National Assembly, the lower house of parliament, was due to vote on the pension funds bill either later on Thursday or early on Friday.

Arthuis has said previously he would like to see the new pension funds, which will be managed independently and meant to complement rather than replace the existing system of universal pensions, set up early next year.
